title: Context engineering: what goes in the window and in what order
story:
The window is a budget, not a container. Everything you put in it competes with everything else, costs money on every request, adds latency on every request, and is an implicit claim that it deserves to be there. The instinct to add one more thing that might help is the instinct to spend, and it never presents itself that way.

Sort what is in yours into three piles and the situation usually becomes clear. There is what must be present for the task to be possible. There is what might plausibly help. And there is what is present because somebody added it once and nobody has removed anything since. In a system that has been running for a while, the third pile is the largest, and nothing in the process ever prompts anyone to look at it.

Then there is the part that is less obvious than volume, which is position.

Liu and colleagues analysed how models use long inputs across two tasks that require finding relevant information in the context — answering questions from multiple documents, and retrieving a value by its key. Performance is often highest when the relevant information occurs at the beginning or the end of the input context, and significantly degrades when the model must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for models built explicitly for long contexts. Their conclusion is stated plainly: current models do not robustly make use of information in long input contexts.

Take that as a design constraint rather than a curiosity, because it changes what you do on an ordinary afternoon of building.

It means a relevant document can be present and effectively unread. Your retrieval can be working perfectly, the evidence can be sitting in the window, and the answer can still miss it because of where it landed. Debugging that by improving retrieval will not work, since retrieval already did its job.

It means adding more can subtract. Passing ten passages instead of five, when the right one was already there, pushes the right one towards the middle of a longer input — so a change that looks like more evidence can be a change that buries the evidence. Quantity is not free even when the window has room, which is the opposite of how a budget with space left tends to be treated.

And it means order is a decision you should be making on purpose. Put the instructions at the start, where they are also stable enough to be reused across requests. Put the evidence in the middle of the structure, ordered best-first, so what retrieval ranked highest sits nearest an edge. Put the question at the end, close to where generation begins. That layout is not a magic arrangement — it is what falls out of the finding, plus the practical matter that a stable beginning is what makes reuse possible at all.

The habit that keeps a window honest is subtraction, and it has to be deliberate because nothing else in the process will ever suggest it. Take a section out, run your cases, and see whether anything changes. Most systems that have been running for a while are carrying a paragraph that was added to fix something that has since been fixed elsewhere, examples that duplicate what the instructions already say, and retrieved text nobody has looked at since the retriever changed. Every one of those is paid for on every request, and the only way it leaves is if somebody removes it.

One more thing worth saying, because it is where this connects to everything else in the track. What goes in the window is the whole of what the model knows at that moment. There is no other channel, no state it carries, nothing it remembers. So context engineering is not a tuning activity around the edges of a system — it is the entire interface between your system and its reasoning, and treating it with less care than you would treat a function signature is a mismatch between how important it is and how it is usually handled.

problem.name: Allocating the context budget
problem.shape: Everything the model can use at this moment has to fit in one input, where each item competes with the rest.
tell: the right document is in the window and the answer ignores it
passing more retrieved passages made the answers worse
nobody can say why a given section of the assembled input is there
the critical instruction sits in the middle of a long stack of retrieved text
problem.move: Treat the window as a budget: keep instructions at the start where they are stable and reusable, place evidence best-first so the strongest sits nearest an edge, put the question at the end, and periodically remove a section and re-run the cases to find what is no longer earning its place.
problem.invariant: Presence is not use — information positioned in the middle of a long input is significantly less likely to be used than the same information at either end.
problem.breaks: Adding more relevant material lengthens the input and pushes what mattered towards the middle, so extra evidence can reduce answer quality even when the window has room.

cost.time: every item is processed on every request, so the window length is directly a latency cost
cost.space: the window is fixed, so each addition is a decision to exclude something else, made implicitly
cost.beats: passing whole documents, which buries the relevant part, and passing only a snippet, which is cheap and frequently insufficient

worked.reasoning:

problem.practice: Take a question your system answers correctly, then pad the input with five more retrieved passages that are relevant but not the one it needs, leaving the necessary passage in place but further from the edges. If the answer degrades, you have reproduced the finding on your own system, and you will never again treat extra context as free.

beats.broke: The window gets treated as a container, so anything that might help is added, nothing is ever removed, and no one accounts for where in the input things land.
beats.fix: Treat it as a budget: stable instructions first, evidence best-first, question last, and a deliberate subtraction pass against a set of cases.
beats.cost: Position matters as much as presence, so more evidence can push what mattered into the middle where it is least likely to be used.

interview.q: What is the context window really, and why can adding a relevant document make an answer worse?
interview.trap: Assuming that if the evidence is in the window, it has been used. Presence is not use — the same passage in the middle of a long input is significantly less likely to be used than at either end.
interview.answer:
It is a budget in which everything competes, not a container. Each item costs money and latency on every request and takes a place something else could have had.

The finding that changes the design is about position. Liu and colleagues analysed multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval and found performance is often highest when the relevant information is at the beginning or end of the input, and degrades significantly when the model must access it in the middle of long contexts — even for explicitly long-context models. Their conclusion is that current models do not robustly use information in long inputs.

So adding a relevant document can make things worse: if the right passage was already there, passing five more lengthens the input and pushes the right one towards the middle. More evidence buries the evidence, and quantity is not free even when there is room.

It also tells me where not to look when debugging. If the evidence was present and unused, retrieval already did its job and improving it changes nothing.

So I order on purpose — instructions first, where they are also stable enough to reuse across requests; evidence best-first so the strongest sits nearest an edge; the question last, close to where generation begins. And I subtract deliberately, removing a section and re-running the cases, because long-running systems accumulate paragraphs that fixed something since fixed elsewhere and examples that restate the instructions, all paid for on every request.

takeaway: The window is a budget where position decides use: information is used best at the beginning or end and significantly less in the middle of a long input, so adding more relevant passages can bury the one that mattered — order deliberately, and subtract on purpose because nothing else ever will.
